theory.question: Message broker vs database: durability, deletion, query model, and change notification.
theory.answer:
A message broker is a specialized datastore optimized for streams: producers append events, the broker notifies consumers, and (in classic JMS/AMQP designs) messages are often deleted after acknowledgment.

Practical differences:
- Lifetime: databases retain until delete; many brokers treat successful delivery as deletion and are poor long-term stores.
- Working set: brokers expect short queues; when consumers lag and the queue spills to disk, per-message latency and throughput often degrade.
- Access: databases expose rich queries and secondary indexes; brokers mainly offer topic/pattern subscriptions.
- Freshness: a DB query is a point-in-time snapshot and will not notify you that a later write invalidated the result; brokers push new messages as they arrive but do not support arbitrary ad-hoc queries or in-place message updates.

Log-based brokers blur the line by keeping an append-only log on disk for hours or weeks so consumers can replay — closer to a database changelog than to a transient RPC queue.

theory.question: Producers outpace consumers on a topic: compare drop, buffer, and backpressure, and say which log-based brokers use.
theory.answer:
When producers emit faster than consumers can process, a messaging system must drop messages, buffer them, or apply backpressure that slows the producer.

Unix pipes and TCP use a small fixed buffer and then block the sender (backpressure). Dropping is acceptable for some metrics or sensor samples where a later reading replaces a lost one, but dangerous for counters and business events. Buffering in a queue absorbs spikes, but you must know whether the queue lives in memory (crash risk when full) or spills to disk (latency and disk-full behavior).

Log-based brokers (Kafka, Kinesis) are large disk-backed buffers: they retain a fixed retention window and effectively drop messages older than that window if a consumer falls too far behind. You monitor consumer lag and alert before the lag exceeds retention so operators can scale or fix the slow consumer. Other consumers are unaffected — a major operational advantage versus traditional brokers that keep per-consumer queues growing forever.

Comment: Prefer backpressure for request/response paths; prefer durable log buffering for async event pipelines where producers should not block on every slow subscriber.

theory.question: Two consumers share a topic: when to use load balancing vs fan-out, and how Kafka consumer groups combine both.
theory.answer:
Load balancing delivers each message to one consumer so workers share processing cost; fan-out delivers each message to every consumer so independent subscribers each see the full stream.

Use load balancing when processing is expensive (image resize, email send, fraud check) and order across the whole topic matters less than throughput. Use fan-out when several independent pipelines need the same events (analytics, search indexing, audit) without interfering — the streaming analogue of multiple batch jobs reading one input file.

Kafka-style consumer groups combine both: within one group, partitions (or messages) are load-balanced so each message is handled once per group; two groups subscribed to the same topic each get a full copy (fan-out across groups). AMQP shared queues and JMS shared subscriptions implement load balancing; topic subscriptions and exchange bindings implement fan-out.

Comment: If causal order for one entity matters (all events for user U), pin that key to one partition/shard and keep load balancing coarse-grained at the shard level.

theory.question: Log-based message brokers: how offsets, partitioning, replay, and retention differ from JMS/AMQP queues.
theory.answer:
A log-based broker stores an append-only partitioned log; producers append, consumers read sequentially by offset, and reading does not delete messages — so you can replay and fan out freely.

Within a partition, messages are totally ordered and get monotonic offsets; there is no order guarantee across partitions. Scale by sharding topics across machines. Load balancing assigns whole partitions to consumers in a group (parallelism capped by partition count); a slow message can head-of-line-block later messages on the same partition. Fan-out is natural: many consumers read the same log independently.

Consumer progress is a single offset checkpoint, not per-message acks — higher throughput, but after a crash the consumer restarts from the last recorded offset and may reprocess some messages (at-least-once). Retention segments delete or archive old data, forming a large circular buffer; fall behind retention and that consumer misses data. Unlike classic brokers, consuming is nondestructive, so you can rewind yesterday's offset and rebuild derived outputs.

Comment: Prefer log brokers for high-throughput ordered streams and data integration; prefer classic queues when you need fine-grained per-message work stealing and ordering is unimportant.

theory.question: Exactly-once (effectively-once) stream processing: microbatching, checkpoints, atomic commit, and idempotence.
theory.answer:
Batch jobs get this by immutable inputs and publishing output only on success. Streams never finish, so frameworks use microbatching (Spark Streaming ~1s blocks) or rolling checkpoints with barriers (Flink): on failure, restore state and discard uncommitted framework-internal output. That alone does not protect external side effects (DB writes, emails, other brokers) — those can fire twice on retry.

Fixes: (1) atomic commit inside one framework that owns both state and messaging (Kafka transactions, Dataflow, VoltDB) so offsets, state, and outputs commit together; (2) idempotent sinks — e.g. store the last Kafka offset with each DB row and skip already-applied offsets. Idempotence needs deterministic replay order, no concurrent writers to the same key, and fencing on failover.

Comment: At-least-once + idempotent upserts is the pragmatic default outside a single transactional stream runtime.

theory.question: Consumer crashes mid-processing: how acknowledgments, redelivery, reordering, and dead-letter queues interact.
theory.answer:
Brokers use acknowledgments so a crash mid-processing does not silently drop work: unacked messages are redelivered, which yields at-least-once delivery and can reorder messages under load balancing.

The ack may be lost even after successful processing, so naive consumers duplicate side effects unless handlers are idempotent or you use an atomic commit protocol for exactly-once effects. With load balancing, redelivery can reorder: consumer 2 dies on m3 while consumer 1 finishes m4, then m3 is later handed to consumer 1 — order becomes m4, m3, m5. Avoid that with a dedicated queue per consumer when order matters.

Poison messages (bad JSON, missing required fields) that always crash consumers create infinite redelivery loops. Dead letter queues (DLQs) move such messages aside so the main queue progresses; operators drop, fix, or replay after inspecting the DLQ.

Comment: Design handlers as idempotent upserts keyed by message id/offset; treat DLQ depth as a paging alert, not a silent trash can.

theory.question: CDC vs event sourcing: define each, how to implement and when to pick each.
theory.answer:
Both turn database change into an ordered stream for derived systems, but they sit at different abstraction levels: CDC extracts low-level mutations from a mutable database; event sourcing makes high-level immutable intent events the system of record.

CDC implementation: attach to the logical replication log / binlog (Debezium, Maxwell, GoldenGate, Kafka Connect sources), emit row-level insert/update/delete events into a log-based broker that preserves order, then sink to search indexes, caches, and warehouses. Bootstrap a new consumer from a consistent snapshot tied to a known log offset (or incremental snapshot watermarking), then stream forward. With primary-keyed changelogs, log compaction keeps the latest value per key so a consumer can rebuild full state from offset 0 without another DB dump. CDC is usually asynchronous — the source commits without waiting for sinks — so expect replication lag. An outbox table written in the same DB transaction as the domain write decouples the public CDC schema from internal tables.

Event sourcing: the app appends immutable intent events; current state is a materialized view from replaying the log (Jim Gray / Andreas Reuter: the log has all the information; the database exists for retrieval performance). Mutable state and the changelog are duals — integrate the stream to get state, differentiate state to get the change stream. Multiple read models (search, timeline cache, analytics) consume the same log independently (CQRS). One user action is one atomic append; a single-threaded consumer per shard needs little write concurrency control. Trade-offs: async consumers mean read-your-writes lag; keep snapshots for fast recovery. Unlike CDC compaction, intent events usually do not overwrite prior events — you need history or snapshots to reconstruct state.

Choose CDC to retrofit sync onto an existing mutable DB with minimal app change; choose event sourcing when you want richer intent history and are willing to redesign writes around the log.

theory.question: Dual writes to a DB and a search index go out of sync: explain the race and the fault case, then how to prevent both.
theory.answer:
Dual writes — the app writes the same change to several systems itself — create races under concurrency and permanent inconsistency when one write fails.

A related trap: writing to an internal table and a CDC outbox in the same database transaction is fine (single atomic commit); writing to Postgres and Elasticsearch in two network calls is the broken dual-write pattern.

Comment: Treat Elasticsearch, caches, and warehouses as followers of one system of record — never as peer leaders updated by ad-hoc app dual writes.

theory.question: Truly deleting data from an immutable log or backups is hard — why, and what techniques help?
theory.answer:
Immutable logs, replicas, caches, snapshots, and backups create many copies of personal data. Deleting the current database row does not remove old log segments, derived indexes, restored backups, or blocks remapped internally by an SSD. Retention policies must therefore be designed into the dataflow rather than added as a final table-level operation.

Useful techniques include compacting logs around tombstones, propagating deletion events to every derived consumer, partitioning data so expired groups can be dropped, and encrypting records with per-user or per-tenant keys that can be destroyed. Backups need an expiry schedule and a documented process that reapplies deletions after restore. Systems should also minimize what they collect and avoid copying identifiers into datasets that do not need them.

No technique makes already leaked plaintext recoverable. The practical goal is a bounded, testable erasure process with an inventory of every durable and derived location.

theory.question: Stream joins: contrast stream–stream, stream–table, and table–table joins with a concrete example of each.
theory.answer:
Stream joins keep local state from one input and probe it with events from the other; the three shapes differ in whether inputs are activity streams or database changelogs.

Stream–table (enrichment): activity events carry user_id; join to a profile table. Prefer a local hash/index copy updated via CDC over per-event remote DB lookups. The table side is a changelog with an infinite window (latest value wins).

Table–table (materialized view): maintain a social home timeline by joining posts and follows changelogs — on new post, fan out to followers' timelines; on follow, backfill recent posts. Equivalent to incrementally maintaining a SQL join grouped by follower.

Time dependence: if streams interleave nondeterministically, joins become nondeterministic on replay; slowly changing dimensions (versioned tax rates) or denormalizing the joined attributes into the event restore determinism.

Comment: Kafka Streams / Flink SQL KStream-KTable joins map directly onto these three patterns.

theory.question: Event time vs processing time for windows: why the distinction matters and how to handle stragglers.
theory.answer:
Event time records when an event occurred at the source; processing time records when a worker handled it. Windowing by processing time turns backlog, retries, and restarts into artificial traffic spikes, while event-time windows preserve the business timeline.

Processors track progress with watermarks: an estimate that no substantially earlier events should still arrive. When the watermark passes a window boundary, the system can emit a result and eventually discard the window state. Because stragglers still occur, the job needs an allowed-lateness policy: drop them, route them to a side output, or revise the prior result with an update or retraction.

Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping; hopping windows overlap at a fixed interval; sliding windows group nearby events; session windows close after an inactivity gap. Larger windows and longer lateness bounds improve completeness but consume more state and delay final results.

practice.task: [RabbitMQ] Bounded queue with backpressure: refuse produce when full
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/ddia-practice:ch12-p0 init
docker compose up -d
# Python deps are preinstalled in the lab image; or: pip install pika>=1.3,<2

# Teardown
docker compose down -v
```

When producers outpace consumers, a messaging system can drop messages, buffer unboundedly, or apply backpressure (block / refuse until the consumer drains). Use RabbitMQ — an open-source AMQP broker — to declare a bounded queue that refuses publishes when full (`x-max-length` + `x-overflow: reject-publish`), then contrast it with drop-head overflow and an unbounded queue.

Prerequisites: Docker with the daemon running, Python 3.10+ with `pip`/`venv`, and RabbitMQ reachable at `localhost:5672` (AMQP) / `http://localhost:15672` (management UI).

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch12_backpressure.py — RabbitMQ bounded queue with produce-side backpressure."""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys

import pika
from pika.exceptions import NackError

HOST = "localhost"
PORT = 5672
MAX_DEPTH = 5

# Three queues: refuse-on-full, drop oldest, unbounded buffer
Q_BOUNDED = "bp.bounded"
Q_DROP = "bp.drop_head"
Q_UNBOUNDED = "bp.unbounded"


class BackpressureError(Exception):
    """Raised when the broker nacks a publish because the bounded queue is full."""


def connect() -> pika.BlockingConnection:
    return pika.BlockingConnection(
        pika.ConnectionParameters(host=HOST, port=PORT, heartbeat=30)
    )


def reset_queues(ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel) -> None:
    """Delete and redeclare the three lab queues (idempotent lab reset)."""
    # Declare with the same arguments as the final lab declare before delete.
    # A bare queue_declare on an existing bounded/drop-head queue raises
    # 406 PRECONDITION_FAILED and closes the channel; delete of a missing
    # queue raises 404 and also closes the channel.
    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_BOUNDED,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "reject-publish",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_BOUNDED)

    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_DROP,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "drop-head",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_DROP)

    ch.queue_declare(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)

    # Bounded: refuse new publishes when full (admission-control backpressure).
    # Publisher confirms are required so the client sees basic.nack.
    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_BOUNDED,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "reject-publish",
        },
    )

    # Same capacity, but default overflow drops the oldest ready message.
    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_DROP,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "drop-head",
        },
    )

    # No length limit — hides a slow consumer until memory/disk hurts.
    ch.queue_declare(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)


def depth(ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel, queue: str) -> int:
    return ch.queue_declare(queue=queue, passive=True).method.message_count


def produce(
    ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel,
    queue: str,
    payload: str,
) -> None:
    """Publish with publisher confirms. On Q_BOUNDED full, raise BackpressureError."""
    # implement:
    # - ch.confirm_delivery() once before publishing on this channel
    # - basic_publish to exchange="" routing_key=queue body=payload.encode()
    # - if the broker nacks (NackError), raise BackpressureError("backpressure: queue full")
    # - other queues should not raise on overflow (drop-head silently drops; unbounded grows)
    raise NotImplementedError


def consume_one(
    ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel,
    queue: str,
) -> str | None:
    """Pull one message with basic_get, ack it, return payload text; None if empty."""
    # implement:
    # - method, props, body = ch.basic_get(queue=queue, auto_ack=False)
    # - if method is None: return None
    # - ch.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag); return body.decode()
    raise NotImplementedError


def fill(ch, queue: str, n: int, prefix: str = "m") -> None:
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        produce(ch, queue, f"{prefix}{i}")


def main() -> None:
    cmd = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "demo"
    conn = connect()
    ch = conn.channel()

    if cmd == "reset":
        reset_queues(ch)
        print("queues reset")
        conn.close()
        return

    if cmd == "demo":
        reset_queues(ch)

        # 1–2: fill bounded to capacity
        fill(ch, Q_BOUNDED, MAX_DEPTH)
        print(f"bounded depth after fill={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # expect 5

        # 3: overflow must fail fast
        try:
            produce(ch, Q_BOUNDED, "overflow")
            print("ERROR: expected BackpressureError")
        except BackpressureError as e:
            print(f"overflow: {e}")
        print(f"bounded depth after reject={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # still 5

        # 4: consume one slot, then produce succeeds
        print(f"consumed={consume_one(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")
        produce(ch, Q_BOUNDED, "m6")
        print(f"bounded depth after drain+produce={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # 5

        # Contrast A: drop-head — 6th publish succeeds; oldest is discarded
        fill(ch, Q_DROP, MAX_DEPTH, prefix="d")
        produce(ch, Q_DROP, "d_new")
        print(f"drop_head depth={depth(ch, Q_DROP)}")  # still 5
        first = consume_one(ch, Q_DROP)
        print(f"drop_head oldest_now={first}")  # expect d2 (d1 was dropped)

        # Contrast B: unbounded — 20 publishes, depth grows
        fill(ch, Q_UNBOUNDED, 20, prefix="u")
        print(f"unbounded depth={depth(ch, Q_UNBOUNDED)}")  # 20

        conn.close()
        return

    print("usage: python3 ch12_backpressure.py [reset|demo]", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Tasks:
1. Start RabbitMQ (Docker command above), create the venv, install `pika`, save `ch12_backpressure.py`.
2. Implement `produce` and `consume_one` at the `# implement` sites. Run `python3 ch12_backpressure.py demo`.
3. Confirm bounded fill reaches depth `5`, `produce(..., "overflow")` raises `BackpressureError: backpressure: queue full`, and depth stays `5`.
4. Confirm after one `consume_one` the next produce (`m6`) succeeds and depth is again `5`.
5. Confirm drop-head keeps depth `5` but the oldest ready message is no longer `d1` (expect `d2`), and unbounded depth is `20`. In 2–4 sentences explain how `reject-publish` backpressure differs from `drop-head` and from an unbounded queue.
practice.answer:
A RabbitMQ queue with `x-max-length` and `x-overflow: reject-publish` turns produce into admission control: when depth hits the limit, the broker nacks the publish (visible only with publisher confirms). `drop-head` keeps capacity by discarding the oldest message; an unbounded queue grows without refusal.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch12_backpressure.py — complete reference"""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys

import pika
from pika.exceptions import NackError

HOST = "localhost"
PORT = 5672
MAX_DEPTH = 5

Q_BOUNDED = "bp.bounded"
Q_DROP = "bp.drop_head"
Q_UNBOUNDED = "bp.unbounded"


class BackpressureError(Exception):
    """Raised when the broker nacks a publish because the bounded queue is full."""


def connect() -> pika.BlockingConnection:
    return pika.BlockingConnection(
        pika.ConnectionParameters(host=HOST, port=PORT, heartbeat=30)
    )


def reset_queues(ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel) -> None:
    """Delete and redeclare the three lab queues (idempotent lab reset)."""
    # Declare with the same arguments as the final lab declare before delete.
    # A bare queue_declare on an existing bounded/drop-head queue raises
    # 406 PRECONDITION_FAILED and closes the channel; delete of a missing
    # queue raises 404 and also closes the channel.
    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_BOUNDED,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "reject-publish",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_BOUNDED)

    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_DROP,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "drop-head",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_DROP)

    ch.queue_declare(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)
    ch.queue_delete(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)

    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_BOUNDED,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "reject-publish",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_declare(
        queue=Q_DROP,
        arguments={
            "x-max-length": MAX_DEPTH,
            "x-overflow": "drop-head",
        },
    )
    ch.queue_declare(queue=Q_UNBOUNDED)


def depth(ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel, queue: str) -> int:
    return ch.queue_declare(queue=queue, passive=True).method.message_count


def produce(
    ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel,
    queue: str,
    payload: str,
) -> None:
    ch.confirm_delivery()
    try:
        ch.basic_publish(
            exchange="",
            routing_key=queue,
            body=payload.encode("utf-8"),
        )
    except NackError as exc:
        raise BackpressureError("backpressure: queue full") from exc


def consume_one(
    ch: pika.adapters.blocking_connection.BlockingChannel,
    queue: str,
) -> str | None:
    method, _props, body = ch.basic_get(queue=queue, auto_ack=False)
    if method is None:
        return None
    ch.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag)
    return body.decode("utf-8")


def fill(ch, queue: str, n: int, prefix: str = "m") -> None:
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        produce(ch, queue, f"{prefix}{i}")


def main() -> None:
    cmd = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "demo"
    conn = connect()
    ch = conn.channel()

    if cmd == "reset":
        reset_queues(ch)
        print("queues reset")
        conn.close()
        return

    if cmd == "demo":
        reset_queues(ch)

        fill(ch, Q_BOUNDED, MAX_DEPTH)
        print(f"bounded depth after fill={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # 5

        try:
            produce(ch, Q_BOUNDED, "overflow")
            print("ERROR: expected BackpressureError")
        except BackpressureError as e:
            print(f"overflow: {e}")
        print(f"bounded depth after reject={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # 5

        print(f"consumed={consume_one(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")
        produce(ch, Q_BOUNDED, "m6")
        print(f"bounded depth after drain+produce={depth(ch, Q_BOUNDED)}")  # 5

        fill(ch, Q_DROP, MAX_DEPTH, prefix="d")
        produce(ch, Q_DROP, "d_new")
        print(f"drop_head depth={depth(ch, Q_DROP)}")  # 5
        first = consume_one(ch, Q_DROP)
        print(f"drop_head oldest_now={first}")  # d2

        fill(ch, Q_UNBOUNDED, 20, prefix="u")
        print(f"unbounded depth={depth(ch, Q_UNBOUNDED)}")  # 20

        conn.close()
        return

    print("usage: python3 ch12_backpressure.py [reset|demo]", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```bash
# Expected demo signals (abridged)
bounded depth after fill=5
overflow: backpressure: queue full
bounded depth after reject=5
consumed=m1
bounded depth after drain+produce=5
drop_head depth=5
drop_head oldest_now=d2
unbounded depth=20
```

Write-up: Unbounded buffering hides a slow consumer until the broker runs out of memory or disk; `drop-head` keeps a fixed buffer but silently discards work (fine for replaceable telemetry, dangerous for business events); `reject-publish` makes overload visible to the producer immediately via `basic.nack` / `BackpressureError` so the caller can slow down, retry, or shed load — the same role as TCP/pipes blocking the sender, expressed as fail-fast admission control.

practice.task: [Kafka] Log-based topic: consumer lag, fan-out groups, and replay
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/ddia-practice:ch12-p1 init
docker compose up -d
# Python deps are preinstalled in the lab image; or: pip install kafka-python>=2.0,<3

# Teardown
docker compose down -v
```

A log-based broker stores an append-only topic: producers append, consumers read by offset, and reading does not delete messages. Unlike a classic queue that can refuse publishes when full, Kafka keeps a disk-backed buffer and tracks per-consumer-group progress as offsets — so a slow group builds lag while other groups still get a full fan-out copy, and any group can rewind to replay.

Prerequisites: Docker with the daemon running, Python 3.10+ with `pip`/`venv`, and Kafka reachable at `localhost:9092`.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch12_log_queue.py — Kafka log-based topic: lag, fan-out groups, replay."""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import time
from typing import Iterable

from kafka import KafkaAdminClient, KafkaConsumer, KafkaProducer, TopicPartition
from kafka.admin import NewTopic
from kafka.errors import TopicAlreadyExistsError, UnknownTopicOrPartitionError

BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"
TOPIC = "ch12.events"
PARTITIONS = 1
GROUP_ANALYTICS = "analytics"
GROUP_INDEXER = "indexer"


def ensure_topic() -> None:
    admin = KafkaAdminClient(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP, client_id="ch12-admin")
    try:
        try:
            admin.delete_topics([TOPIC])
            time.sleep(2.0)
        except UnknownTopicOrPartitionError:
            pass
        try:
            admin.delete_consumer_groups([GROUP_ANALYTICS, GROUP_INDEXER])
            time.sleep(1.0)
        except Exception:
            pass
        try:
            admin.create_topics(
                [NewTopic(name=TOPIC, num_partitions=PARTITIONS, replication_factor=1)]
            )
            time.sleep(1.0)
        except TopicAlreadyExistsError:
            pass
    finally:
        admin.close()


def produce_all(payloads: Iterable[str]) -> int:
    """Append payloads to TOPIC; return count written. Never refuse for consumer lag."""
    producer = KafkaProducer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP,
        acks="all",
        key_serializer=lambda k: k.encode("utf-8") if k is not None else None,
        value_serializer=lambda v: v.encode("utf-8"),
    )
    n = 0
    for payload in payloads:
        # single partition + constant key keeps total order for the lab
        producer.send(TOPIC, key="k", value=payload)
        n += 1
    producer.flush()
    producer.close()
    return n


def _consumer(group_id: str) -> KafkaConsumer:
    return KafkaConsumer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP,
        group_id=group_id,
        auto_offset_reset="earliest",
        enable_auto_commit=False,
        key_deserializer=lambda b: b.decode("utf-8") if b else None,
        value_deserializer=lambda b: b.decode("utf-8"),
    )


def drain_group(group_id: str, idle_ms: int = 1500) -> list[str]:
    """Subscribe as group_id; read until idle; commit; return payloads in order."""
    # implement:
    # - subscribe to TOPIC; poll until assignment is non-empty
    # - if committed(tp) is None for an assigned partition, seek to beginning
    #   (assignment polls can fetch+discard and leave the cursor at log end)
    # - poll until idle_ms with no records; append values; commit after each batch
    # - close and return the payloads
    raise NotImplementedError
```

Kafka appends to a durable partitioned log: produce keeps succeeding while a group lags, each consumer group tracks its own offset (fan-out across groups), and seek rewinds for replay because consume is nondestructive.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch12_log_queue.py — Kafka log-based topic: lag, fan-out groups, replay."""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import time
from typing import Iterable

from kafka import KafkaAdminClient, KafkaConsumer, KafkaProducer
from kafka.admin import NewTopic
from kafka.errors import TopicAlreadyExistsError, UnknownTopicOrPartitionError

BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"
TOPIC = "ch12.events"
PARTITIONS = 1
GROUP_ANALYTICS = "analytics"
GROUP_INDEXER = "indexer"


def ensure_topic() -> None:
    admin = KafkaAdminClient(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP, client_id="ch12-admin")
    try:
        try:
            admin.delete_topics([TOPIC])
            time.sleep(2.0)
        except UnknownTopicOrPartitionError:
            pass
        try:
            admin.delete_consumer_groups([GROUP_ANALYTICS, GROUP_INDEXER])
            time.sleep(1.0)
        except Exception:
            pass
        try:
            admin.create_topics(
                [NewTopic(name=TOPIC, num_partitions=PARTITIONS, replication_factor=1)]
            )
            time.sleep(1.0)
        except TopicAlreadyExistsError:
            pass
    finally:
        admin.close()


def produce_all(payloads: Iterable[str]) -> int:
    """Append payloads to TOPIC; return count written. Never refuse for consumer lag."""
    producer = KafkaProducer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP,
        acks="all",
        key_serializer=lambda k: k.encode("utf-8") if k is not None else None,
        value_serializer=lambda v: v.encode("utf-8"),
    )
    n = 0
    for payload in payloads:
        producer.send(TOPIC, key="k", value=payload)
        n += 1
    producer.flush()
    producer.close()
    return n


def _consumer(group_id: str) -> KafkaConsumer:
    return KafkaConsumer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP,
        group_id=group_id,
        auto_offset_reset="earliest",
        enable_auto_commit=False,
        key_deserializer=lambda b: b.decode("utf-8") if b else None,
        value_deserializer=lambda b: b.decode("utf-8"),
    )


def drain_group(group_id: str, idle_ms: int = 1500) -> list[str]:
    """
    Subscribe as group_id from committed offset (or earliest if none).
    Collect values until idle_ms with no new records; commit; return payloads in order.
    """
    consumer = _consumer(group_id)
    consumer.subscribe([TOPIC])
    out: list[str] = []
    assigned = False
    idle_deadline: float | None = None
    join_deadline = time.time() + 20.0

    while True:
        batch = consumer.poll(timeout_ms=400)
        if not assigned:
            if consumer.assignment():
                assigned = True
                # Assignment polls can fetch+discard and leave the cursor at log end
                # even when there is no committed offset. Rewind only for a new group.
                seeked = False
                for tp in consumer.assignment():
                    if consumer.committed(tp) is None:
                        consumer.seek(tp, consumer.beginning_offsets([tp])[tp])
                        seeked = True
                if seeked:
                    batch = {}
                idle_deadline = None
            elif time.time() > join_deadline:
                consumer.close()
                raise RuntimeError("timed out waiting for partition assignment")
            else:
                continue

        if not batch:
            if idle_deadline is None:
                idle_deadline = time.time() + idle_ms / 1000.0
            elif time.time() >= idle_deadline:
                break
            continue

        idle_deadline = None
        for _tp, msgs in batch.items():
            for msg in msgs:
                out.append(msg.value)
        consumer.commit()

    consumer.close()
    return out


def consumer_lag(group_id: str) -> int:
    """Sum (end_offset - committed_offset) across partitions for group_id."""
    consumer = _consumer(group_id)
    # Avoid subscribe+poll (that can fetch). Use committed offsets API via assign.
    partitions = []
    # Discover partition count from a short-lived consumer
    meta = KafkaConsumer(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP)
    parts = meta.partitions_for_topic(TOPIC) or set()
    meta.close()
    from kafka import TopicPartition

    tps = [TopicPartition(TOPIC, p) for p in sorted(parts)]
    consumer.assign(tps)
    ends = consumer.end_offsets(tps)
    lag = 0
    for tp in tps:
        committed = consumer.committed(tp)
        start = committed if committed is not None else 0
        lag += ends[tp] - start
    consumer.close()
    return lag


def replay_from_beginning(group_id: str, idle_ms: int = 1500) -> list[str]:
    """Seek the group's partitions to earliest and drain again (nondestructive log read)."""
    consumer = _consumer(group_id)
    consumer.subscribe([TOPIC])
    deadline = time.time() + 20.0
    while not consumer.assignment() and time.time() < deadline:
        consumer.poll(timeout_ms=200)
    if not consumer.assignment():
        consumer.close()
        raise RuntimeError("timed out waiting for partition assignment")
    consumer.seek_to_beginning()

    out: list[str] = []
    idle_deadline: float | None = None
    while True:
        batch = consumer.poll(timeout_ms=400)
        if not batch:
            if idle_deadline is None:
                idle_deadline = time.time() + idle_ms / 1000.0
            elif time.time() >= idle_deadline:
                break
            continue
        idle_deadline = None
        for _tp, msgs in batch.items():
            for msg in msgs:
                out.append(msg.value)
        consumer.commit()
    consumer.close()
    return out


def main() -> None:
    cmd = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "demo"
    if cmd == "reset":
        ensure_topic()
        print("topic reset")
        return

    if cmd == "demo":
        ensure_topic()

        n = produce_all([f"m{i}" for i in range(1, 6)])
        print(f"produced={n}")  # 5 — succeeds even with no consumers

        analytics = drain_group(GROUP_ANALYTICS)
        print(f"analytics_first={analytics}")  # ['m1', ..., 'm5']
        print(f"analytics_lag_after={consumer_lag(GROUP_ANALYTICS)}")  # 0

        n2 = produce_all([f"m{i}" for i in range(6, 9)])
        print(f"produced_more={n2}")  # 3
        print(f"analytics_lag_behind={consumer_lag(GROUP_ANALYTICS)}")  # 3

        indexer = drain_group(GROUP_INDEXER)
        print(f"indexer_all={indexer}")  # m1..m8
        print(f"analytics_still_lag={consumer_lag(GROUP_ANALYTICS)}")  # still 3

        caught = drain_group(GROUP_ANALYTICS)
        print(f"analytics_catchup={caught}")  # m6..m8
        replayed = replay_from_beginning(GROUP_ANALYTICS)
        print(f"analytics_replay={replayed}")  # m1..m8
        return

    print("usage: python3 ch12_log_queue.py [reset|demo]", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```bash
analytics_lag_after=0
```

Write-up: A classic bounded queue applies produce-side backpressure (or drops) when full; a log-based broker buffers on disk and signals overload as consumer lag against a retention window instead of refusing the producer. Independent groups each keep an offset, so analytics can lag while indexer replays the same topic from the start — fan-out without copying into per-subscriber queues. Rewinding with `seek_to_beginning` works because reading never deletes the log, unlike competing-consumer AMQP queues where an ack removes the message.

practice.answer:
Kafka delivers at-least-once: after a lost ack the group rewinds and redelivers. A naive balance update double-applies; an offset-guarded upsert that stores `msg.offset` on the account row keeps one visible effect — effectively-once via idempotence, with the Kafka commit after the DB write.

```sql
-- ch12_eos_setup.sql — Postgres sink for Kafka effectively-once lab
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS eos CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA eos;

CREATE TABLE eos.accounts (
  account_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance_cents BIGINT NOT NULL,
  last_offset BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT -1
);
INSERT INTO eos.accounts (account_id, balance_cents) VALUES ('alice', 0);
```

Write-up: `simulate_lost_ack` rewinds the Kafka consumer-group offset without undoing Postgres — the same failure mode as a crash after the DB write but before `consumer.commit()`. `consume_idempotent` stores the Kafka offset on the sink row and skips already-applied offsets (include the offset with the value). Committing the Kafka offset only after the guarded UPDATE is the pragmatic ack-after-side-effect ordering; a production stream runtime can still add fencing for zombie consumers and atomic offset+state commit via Kafka transactions or Flink/Kafka Streams EOS.
